# Pisot and Salem values in a group generated by arbitrarily many small inputs

<a id="statement"></a>
## What mixing the inputs can add

There is an absolute \(\varepsilon>0\) with the following properties.
Take any family of nontorsion algebraic units \(w_i\) with \(0<m(w_i)<\varepsilon\), with \(m=\log M\) in total normalization, and let \(\Gamma=D(\{w_i\})\) consist of torsion twists and radicals of finite integer monomials in their conjugates.
The family may be infinite, its members may have coincident or intersecting conjugate groups, and the sum of their measures need not be bounded.

There is no Pisot number in \(\Gamma\).
The primitive positive real Salem numbers in \(\Gamma\) are exactly the union of those in the individual \(D(w_i)\).
Each such primitive value \(\sigma\) is supplied by the terminal compressed block product of at least one individual input, with \(\log\sigma\le m(w_i)\) and \(\deg\sigma\le\deg w_i\) for that input.
The set of possible terminal fixed values of bounded Mahler orbits of nontorsion members of \(\Gamma\) consists precisely of the positive integral powers of these Salem numbers.
If the list is empty, every such orbit tends to infinity.

In particular a uniform gap for Mahler measures of **integer polynomials whose own sequence of iterates stays bounded** is equivalent to the real Salem gap.
Here the first iterate of \(P\) is \(M(P)\) and all subsequent iterations are applied to that algebraic number.
The equivalence permits arbitrarily many irreducible factors and arbitrarily large bounds on different individual orbits.
For each sufficiently small positive \(m(P)\) in this class a primitive Salem unit of log measure at most \(m(P)\) actually lies in the divisible group of the conjugates of the roots of a single irreducible factor of \(P\).

<a id="counts"></a>
## Removing independent components without increasing the counts

It suffices to work with a finite subfamily supporting a given nontorsion \(x\).
Apply the [combined constituent decomposition](Yin_C_G0901_v118.md#modules): coincident leading spaces of chain terms are identified, and distinct actual leading spaces \(W\) are pairwise nonisomorphic simple submodules.
Each is attached to a compressed chain term \(z\), of small measure no greater than that of its original input, with kernel field equal to the splitting field of \(z\).
The resulting \(z\)'s for different \(W\)'s are unmatched.
The splitting field of the torsion-class product of \(x\) is the compositum of these fields for the active \(W\)'s.
This follows from intersection of the kernels on the direct sum; the compression itself preserves the full span.
Compress \(x\) and count the conjugates in each of the closed regions \(|\cdot|\ge1\) and \(|\cdot|\le1\).
Neither count increases on compression, by constancy of modulus within each torsion class.

If at least two active spaces remain, choose one of largest attached compressed degree \(d\).
Inside the compositum of their attached splitting fields take the normal subgroup \(N\) fixing the fields attached to all the other active spaces.
At the common measure bound one the [unmatched-field theorem](Yin_C_G0901_v87.md#statement) gives a nontrivial supported alternating permutation in the projection of \(N\) on the labels of the chosen input.
All the degrees exceed its threshold for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) by bounded-degree coefficient finiteness, and tied largest degrees are allowed.
This permutation acts nontrivially on the chosen \(W\) because its action is faithful there, whereas \(N\) fixes all the other active spaces.
Normality and irreducibility make \(W^N=0\).
The product of the distinct members of the current \(N\)-orbit is a nonzero class with exactly the other components, multiplied by the positive orbit size.
Its conjugates are products over disjoint \(N\)-orbits, possibly with repetitions among the products.
Both closed-region counts therefore do not increase, just as in the [single-chain norm argument](Yin_C_G0901_v115.md#norm).
Compress once more and repeat.

When a single \(W\) remains, let \(b\) be the block size of its attached \(z\).
The [pure-space orbit and height estimate](Yin_C_G0901_v115.md#pure) bounds both counts of the final unit, and hence of \(x\), below by \((b-1)/4\).
The minimum possible \(b\) tends uniformly to infinity as \(\sup_i m(w_i)\to0\), with no dependence on the number of inputs used.
Taking it greater than five rules out any Pisot unit, which would have just one conjugate on the closed exterior side.
All elements of \(\Gamma\) are units.

<a id="values"></a>
## Recovering a single original factor for the bounded-orbit problem

If \(\Gamma\) contains a real Salem number then it contains the primitive positive Salem generator \(\sigma\) on its unit line in its real root field.
The function \(g\mapsto\log|g\sigma|\) in a common finite normal closure is a nonzero rational linear combination of the translated log functions of finitely many original \(w_i\).
Taking its inner product with itself thus detects a Salem conjugate from at least one individual \(w_i\).
The [projection theorem](Yin_C_G0901_v52.md#statement) gives \(\log\sigma\le m(w_i)\) after decreasing \(\varepsilon\).
Now apply the [quantitative unmatched comparison](Yin_C_G0901_v118.md#quantitative) to the positive Perron unit \(\sigma\) in the combined span.
Its proof only uses the active constituent fields, the small measures of their attached representatives and the orbit of the actual compressed target; it also applies here because \(\sigma\) is itself compressed.
If it fails to match a representative of largest active degree \(d\), it gives \(m(\sigma)m(z)\gg d/(\log(3d))^{212}\).
This is impossible since both measures are at most \(\varepsilon\) and \(d\) is uniformly large.
So \(\sigma\) matches a single chain term and belongs to that original \(D(w_i)\).
The [individual Salem-line theorem](Yin_C_G0901_v113.md#salem) now supplies the terminal term and both bounds for that same input.
The reverse containment of the individual lists is immediate.

Every bounded orbit of a fixed nontorsion \(x\) stabilizes, since it is nondecreasing after the first step and its values lie in the locally finite measure spectrum of \(D(x)\). [Local finiteness](Yin_C_G0901_v96.md#count)
A fixed nontrivial positive unit must be Pisot or Salem, and the positive Salem powers themselves are fixed. [Fixed units](Yin_C_G0901_v113.md#iteration)
This proves the assertions about terminal values and divergence.
For \(P\) sufficiently close to measure one, only monic unit factors can contribute; their positive log measures sum to \(m(P)\), counted with multiplicity.
The positive exterior product \(M(P)\) lies in their common \(\Gamma\).
If its orbit is bounded, the preceding argument yields the indicated primitive Salem generator from an individual factor, with log measure at most that factor's measure.
Conversely any sequence of Salem numbers tending to one gives their integer minimal polynomials with bounded, indeed fixed-after-first-step, orbits.
